title: Arbitral Tribunal Cuts Rs 3,177 Crore Claim Against NHAI to Rs 46 Crore Over Bareilly-Sitapur Toll Road
meta_description: A tribunal allows only three of thirty claims by the Bareilly-Sitapur BOT concessionaire, finding the project delays were concurrent, not NHAI's alone.
court: Arbitral Tribunal (ad hoc, constituted under the concession agreement)
bench: Three-member Arbitral Tribunal; composition not disclosed in available public reporting
case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. Bareilly Highways Project Limited
citation: Arbitral award disclosed via official NHAI statement issued 27 July 2026; exact date of signing of the award not disclosed in public reporting
body: A concessionaire that terminated its concession agreement with the National Highways Authority of India in 2019 and went after it for over three thousand crore rupees has come away with less than two per cent of what it asked for. An Arbitral Tribunal has allowed only three of the thirty claims raised by Bareilly Highways Project Limited, totalling about Rs 46 crore plus applicable interest, against a demand of roughly Rs 3,177 crore, in an award disclosed through an official NHAI statement issued on 27 July 2026.

The dispute goes back to the Bareilly-Sitapur BOT toll project in Uttar Pradesh, a 151-kilometre highway stretch that NHAI terminated in May 2019. The concessionaire behind the project, Bareilly Highways Project Limited, is a company promoted by Era Infra Engineering. Once the concession ended, BHPL took the dispute to arbitration, raising thirty separate claims that together ran into the thousands of crores, covering losses it said it suffered over the life of the project and on termination.

Central to the Tribunal's reasoning was a Supplementary Agreement dated 30 March 2015, which it treated as governing the parties' rights and obligations for the period in dispute. Working from that agreement, the Tribunal concluded that the delays which plagued the project were concurrent, meaning both NHAI and the concessionaire bore responsibility for the slippages, rather than the fault lying with NHAI alone as BHPL's claims assumed. That single finding did most of the work in the award. Once the delays were treated as shared rather than attributable to NHAI, the bulk of BHPL's claims for losses flowing from those delays had no basis to stand on.

The Tribunal did not reject every claim outright. It allowed three of the thirty, worth about Rs 46 crore together with applicable interest, while dismissing the remaining twenty-seven. NHAI did not come away with everything it wanted either. It had filed counterclaims against BHPL, and the Tribunal declined to allow any of those as well. The net result leaves BHPL with a small fraction of what it sought, and NHAI without any affirmative recovery of its own, though NHAI's own public statement framed the outcome squarely as a win given how far short the allowed amount fell of the claimed amount.

What the reporting does not establish is as significant as what it does. None of the available accounts name the members of the three-person Tribunal, and none reproduce the award's text beyond the figures and the concurrent-delay finding that NHAI's statement chose to highlight. The coverage traces back almost entirely to that one official statement, repeated across multiple outlets with only minor variation in phrasing. Whether BHPL intends to challenge the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, as concessionaires in comparable NHAI disputes have done before, is not something the current reporting addresses.

Even allowing for that gap, the award fits a pattern that has become familiar in India's highway sector. BOT concessionaires terminated mid-contract routinely value their claims in the thousands of crores, covering lost equity returns, unrecovered debt, and the premium they say they would have earned over the remaining concession period. NHAI, as respondent in most of these references, has an equally consistent record of arguing that the termination was justified and the claimed losses inflated. Awards like this one, where a tribunal accepts NHAI's characterisation of the delay as shared rather than solely attributable to the authority, tend to gut such claims almost entirely, since concurrent delay findings cut off compensation for the downstream consequences of delay regardless of which party ultimately terminated the contract.

For concessionaires sizing up whether to pursue termination claims against NHAI, the case is a reminder that the size of the claim filed bears little relation to what a tribunal is likely to award once it works through the delay history on the facts. For NHAI, which answers to the public exchequer for every rupee it pays out on terminated BOT contracts, an award of this kind is the outcome it will point to whenever a similarly large claim is filed against it elsewhere.
why_it_matters: NHAI faces a steady stream of multi-thousand-crore arbitration claims from concessionaires whose BOT contracts were terminated, and how tribunals treat delay attribution decides most of these cases. A concurrent-delay finding, as here, can reduce a claim by well over ninety per cent regardless of its headline size. Concessionaires preparing termination claims, and the authority defending them, both need to reckon with how much weight a tribunal is likely to put on shared responsibility for project delays before litigating the quantum.
card_summary: A tribunal slashes a Rs 3,177 crore claim against NHAI over the terminated Bareilly-Sitapur toll project to about Rs 46 crore, finding the delays were concurrent rather than NHAI's alone.
card_tip: In BOT termination arbitrations, a concurrent-delay finding can wipe out the bulk of a concessionaire's claim regardless of its headline value; delay attribution usually decides the quantum.
verification_notes: Confirmed via four independent outlets (NBM&CW, Devdiscourse, Indian Masterminds, The Shillong Times via PTI) reporting consistent figures: Rs 3,177 crore claimed across 30 claims, Rs 46 crore plus interest allowed across 3 claims, the Supplementary Agreement of 30 March 2015, the concurrent-delay finding, the May 2019 termination, and the rejection of NHAI's counterclaims. All available coverage traces to a single NHAI official statement dated 27 July 2026; no independent report of the Tribunal's reasoning or composition was found, and this is flagged rather than filled in with invented detail. The precise date on which the award itself was signed is not given in any source; the announcement date is used as decision_date and this is noted here rather than presented as the award date.
